newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - Mergers seen boosting European aerospace.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Mergers seen boosting European aerospace.

text.p: Mergers would help boost the power Europe's defence and aerospace industry in the face of fierce competition from the United States, EU Industrial Affairs Commissioner Martin Bangemann said on Tuesday.
"Every merger...is a step forward to greater competitiveness," Bangemann told a conference on the future of Europe's aerospace industry.
He said the European Commission, the EU's executive, was prepared to help create an industrial structure that would make Europe competitive on world markets.

Aerospace industry chiefs agreed the need to restructure the sector, which has struggled with overcapacity and structural problems since the end of the Cold War and a serious slump in orders for civilian aircraft in the early 1990s.
Currently, the industry consists of 12 large companies, each employing more than 10,000 people. There are also some 700 firms operating as contractors and suppliers.
British Aerospace president Sir Richard Evans said there was increasing pressure to restructure in the face of mega-mergers in the United States and increasing global competition.
"Europe, however, remains fragmented and in order to be able to compete in world markets, the European aerospace industry must move forward towards trans-national structures," he said.
The favoured way for restructuring the industry was to replace loose cooperative agreements with transnational firms.
"To achieve this, we need to put the whole industry into the hands of the private market sector and free the tax-payer from the burden of annual subsidies," he said.

Daimler-Benz Aerospace (DASA) head Manfred Bischoff said national European companies would not be able to bear the financial and technological risks associated with the development of high-tech aerospace products.

"We know that trans-national mergers -- a Europeanisation -- will have to take place, but here the pace is clearly dictated by our governments. That makes our structural problem a political issue," he said.
European Commission President Jacques Santer said there was an unnecessary number of programmes. In aeronautics 10 European firms were producing helicopters and military aircraft and eleven missiles.
"There are only five in each case producing the same hardware in the U.S. -- who can therefore benefit from scale economies," he said.

At the conference, industry speakers -- looking for increased EU support in funding research -- said there was a need for "a stronger partnership" between public authorities and aerospace companies in view of Washington's commitment to support the supremacy of its industry.
Bischoff talked about "the enormous gap" between government research funding on the two sides of the Atlantic.
"Today, Europe is falling seriously behind the rest of the world in its investment in research and technology, so important for future competitiveness," said Evans at British Aerospace.

"If Europe is therefore to retain a competitive aerospace industry, it has no choice but to match the support of the competition in a coherent fashion. This means Community support and member state support," he said.

The industry, through the European Association of Aerospace Industries, also called for a new Single European Aviation Authority to support the competitiveness of Europe's aircraft industry as well as a long-term EU policy for sustainable growth of air transport.
